Its iterative dynamic variant (cvrp_parallel_merge_dynamic/v1) has ~25 ms p95 and would consume >5% of budget but is structurally riskier at scale, whereas static stays ultra-fast (~7 ms p95, ~7.3 ms on n=200) with 100% completion and huge headroom under the 500 ms budget. The sequential construct template (cvrp_sequential_construct/v1) lags CW by ~10.7% remaining gap on dev_24, so it would waste evolution budget. Choosing static parallel merge gives the best quality head start with negligible timing pressure, leaving ample budget for evolution of merge heuristics or fast post-processing.

import numpy as np

def score_merge_static(distance_matrix, demands, capacity, i_idx, j_idx):
    """Return a 1D array of finite float priority scores (higher = merge earlier)."""
    lam = 1.0
    mu = 0.15
    demand_weight = 0.1

    d0i = distance_matrix[0, i_idx]
    d0j = distance_matrix[0, j_idx]
    dij = distance_matrix[i_idx, j_idx]

    savings = d0i + d0j - lam * dij + mu * np.abs(d0i - d0j)

    scale = np.mean(distance_matrix[0, 1:])
    if not np.isfinite(scale) or scale <= 0:
        scale = 1.0

    demand_fill = (demands[i_idx] + demands[j_idx]) / capacity
    demand_fill = np.clip(demand_fill, 0.0, 1.0)

    scores = savings / scale + demand_weight * demand_fill
    return scores
